terms.definition: The movement of a solute from one side of a membrane to the other. The everyday sense of transport, goods carried somewhere in a vehicle that travels, survives only in the part about getting from one place to another: what moves a solute here is a protein fixed in the membrane, which goes nowhere itself. This is a different process from the vesicular transport of PREM-BIO-003, where a membrane-bounded container really does travel between compartments.

Movement of a solute across a lipid bilayer by dissolving in it and diffusing through, with no protein involved and no energy source beyond the solute's own concentration difference. Available to small nonpolar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide, and much more slowly to small uncharged polar molecules such as water and urea. Ions are effectively excluded.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-002 owns diffusion as the spreading of molecules by random thermal motion with no motor or flow, and that meaning is kept unchanged here. This lesson narrows it to the particular case of that motion carrying a solute across a bilayer unaided, which is one of the four transport routes it classifies. The mean-square-displacement behaviour taught in the earlier lesson still governs the motion; nothing about it is revised.

terms.definition: Protein-mediated movement of a solute down its own electrochemical gradient, requiring no energy source beyond that gradient. It covers all channel proteins and many carrier proteins, so it is not the name of a mechanism but of an energetic category: a channel and a carrier can both be doing it. GLUT2 carrying glucose out of an enterocyte and an aquaporin passing water are both examples. Passive transport is the broader category and not another name for this one: it also covers simple diffusion straight through the bilayer, which needs no protein at all. Every instance of facilitated diffusion is passive; not every passive movement is facilitated.

alignment.note: A narrowing of the diffusion sense PREM-BIO-002 owns, to the case where a membrane protein provides the path while the direction and the driving force still come from the solute's own gradient. The word facilitated marks the protein, not any added energy, which is the distinction this lesson's classification turns on. Passive transport is recorded as an alias because the source establishing the category treats the two names as the same thing.

terms.definition: Movement of a solute against its own electrochemical gradient, which requires free energy from a source other than that gradient. Cells drive it in three ways: coupled carriers spend the downhill movement of a second solute, ATP-driven pumps split ATP, and light-driven pumps use absorbed light. The word active refers to the requirement for outside energy and not specifically to ATP, which is the point most easily lost.

Active transport in which the protein moving the solute is itself the protein that consumes the energy source, which in animal cells means it hydrolyses ATP. The sodium-potassium ATPase is the example this lesson uses. A cell deprived of ATP loses primary active transport essentially at once, because the molecule being consumed has gone.

Active transport in which the protein moving the solute uphill spends an ion's electrochemical gradient rather than splitting ATP itself. ATP hydrolysis is coupled to the transport only indirectly, through that gradient, and it happens in a different protein. SGLT1 is the example here: it moves glucose uphill and has no ATP-hydrolysing step, so it keeps working after ATP is gone until the gradient it depends on has run down.

The net driving force on a solute across a membrane, obtained by combining the contribution of its concentration difference with the contribution of the membrane potential acting on its charge. For an uncharged solute only the first contribution exists. For an ion both must be counted, and in the enterocyte of this lesson the voltage contribution is the larger of the two, so a concentration ratio alone understates the driving force on sodium.

The difference in electrical potential between the inside of a cell and the fluid outside it, conventionally quoted as inside minus outside and normally negative in an animal cell. It supplies the electrical half of the electrochemical gradient. The sodium-potassium ATPase contributes to it by removing one net positive charge per cycle, though it is not the only contributor.

A coupled carrier that moves two solutes across a membrane in the same direction, so that the downhill movement of one can drive the uphill movement of the other. SGLT1 is a symporter for sodium and glucose. The broader word cotransporter covers symporters together with antiporters, so it is not interchangeable with this one.

A coupled carrier that moves two solutes across a membrane in opposite directions, one downhill and the other uphill. Named here to complete the direction vocabulary; no antiporter is worked through in this lesson.
A carrier that transports a single solute across a membrane and is coupled to nothing else. GLUT2 moving glucose alone is the example in this lesson.

The number of coupling ions a transporter moves for each molecule of its substrate, per transport cycle. Two sodium ions per glucose for SGLT1, one for SGLT2. It is the parameter that sets how far uphill a substrate can be driven: the free-energy budget is directly proportional to it, and because that budget enters through an exponent, the largest attainable concentration ratio varies as the coupling ion's concentration ratio raised to this number.

The sodium-glucose cotransporter of the small-intestinal brush-border membrane, which carries one glucose molecule inward together with two sodium ions. It is a secondary active transporter: it can concentrate glucose inside the cell above the luminal level, and it does so by spending the sodium electrochemical gradient maintained by the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase rather than by splitting ATP.

A relative of SGLT1 found in the kidney, whose sodium to glucose coupling ratio is one to one rather than two to one. Used in this lesson only as a real instance of a different coupling stoichiometry, so that the consequence of changing that number is a statement about actual proteins.

A low-affinity, high-capacity facilitative glucose carrier of the enterocyte. At low luminal glucose it sits in the basolateral membrane, where it lets glucose leave towards the blood downhill and uncoupled, by facilitated diffusion. At high luminal glucose it is also reported in the brush-border membrane, so one transporter per face is a common condition rather than a rule.

The ATP-splitting carrier of the plasma membrane that exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions for every ATP molecule hydrolysed. In the enterocyte it sits in the basolateral membrane, where it keeps cytosolic sodium low and, by removing one net positive charge per cycle, contributes to holding the cell interior negative. It builds the gradient that every sodium-coupled transporter in the cell then spends.

A compound that inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase specifically. It is used in this lesson as an experimental tool: because it acts on the pump in the basolateral membrane and not on the apical cotransporter, the fact that it stops brush-border glucose transport shows that the effect travels through the sodium gradient rather than through any contact with the transporter itself.

The movement of water across a membrane in response to a difference in effective osmolality, from the side where water is less constrained by solute towards the side where it is more so. Water is moved this way and is not pumped: no protein drives water against its own gradient, so the only way a cell shifts water is by shifting solute and letting water follow.

A channel protein that lets water cross a membrane along an osmotic gradient. Aquaporins are one of three routes discussed for water crossing an epithelium, alongside movement carried by cotransporters and movement between cells through the tight junctions; how the total divides between the three is not settled.

The two ways something can cross an epithelial sheet: through the cells, entering at one face and leaving at the other, or between the cells, past the tight junctions. Glucose absorption in this lesson is transcellular throughout. Water is thought to use both, and claudin-2 and claudin-15 have been identified as molecular components of the paracellular water route.

The enterotoxin secreted by Vibrio cholerae, which is not itself invasive. Its catalytic subunit transfers ADP-ribose onto the stimulatory G protein's alpha subunit, disabling that protein's ability to switch itself off, so adenylate cyclase runs without pause and cyclic AMP stays high. The toxin does not kill the cell it acts on, and the epithelium stays structurally intact, which is why absorption remains possible.

A chloride channel of the apical membrane. Protein kinase A, activated by high cyclic AMP, phosphorylates it and increases chloride secretion into the lumen; water then follows that chloride osmotically. Named here as the route the secretion runs through, in contrast with the coupled absorptive route that raised cyclic AMP leaves alone.

Treatment of dehydration from diarrhoeal illness by giving a solution of salt and glucose by mouth, so that sodium is absorbed through the intact glucose-coupled cotransport route and water follows osmotically. It replaces what is being lost: the standard glucose-based solution does not stop the secretion, shorten the illness, or clear the infection. The therapy is the practice and the solution is the substance it uses, so the two are not interchangeable words. Discussed in this lesson strictly as the setting for a transport mechanism, with no composition, dose, or regimen stated anywhere.
